title: Product-Led Schools
author: John Danner
summary: John Danner, who runs the Flourish school model after founding Rocketship, argues that we are entering an era of product-led schools in which technology designs each student's learning and teachers deliver it. He explains that earlier attempts such as Summit Learning failed because the software was blind, whereas today's product can transcribe classrooms and see how students work, struggle and interact. His case for the model is cultural: if pedagogy lives in the product, schools can hire adults for how they show up for children, not for lesson-design skill, widening the pool, removing human capital as a growth constraint and making institutional knowledge less fragile. He offers early evidence from fifteen-minute one-on-one interventions that the product schedules and scripts, though the sample is only a few dozen. He expects school leaders to build their own products with AI, so that their job shifts from hiring and training teachers to building the product that fits their school.
points: The claimed change since Summit Learning is awareness: classroom transcripts let the product see process, not just work submitted.
Separating lesson design (product) from delivery (adults) lets schools hire for warmth and presence rather than credentials.
Danner points to PBL, where he says only about 10% of teachers design well but most can deliver a well-designed project.
Product-led schools would expand the pool of potential teachers and remove human capital as the limit on growth.
The evidence offered is thin (a few dozen interventions) and comes from the author's own schools, and the privacy trade-off rests on parental consent.
quotes: I believe that we are entering the era of product-led schools: schools where product designs the learning and teachers deliver it. By product, I mean the technology that plans each student’s lessons, adapts to what they know, and gets better every week. Teachers still do the most important work in the building. They just stop doing the work most of them were never set up to do well.

Today, product can be aware of everything going on. At Flourish, we transcribe our classroom and use that to understand not just the work students are submitting, but how they are doing it, where they are struggling, how they are interacting with peers and teachers. Product now has a full picture of each student.

When you are product-led, you can hire for the thing that matters most, which is how an adult shows up for students every day. Pedagogical design lives in the product, so you no longer have to find people who are great at both designing lessons and connecting with students. Teachers may not be certified or have a fancy degree, but they are there for the right reasons and excited to help children. Because teachers are with kids so many hours each day, their attitude about the students they support is more important than any other factor.

Product decides, based on student work, when a teacher should conduct an intervention and gives them the lesson plan. The intervention is fifteen minutes and completely customized to what that student needs, with a teacher-student time, student-only time, and teacher-student review.

PBL was almost always teacher-designed in the past, but the learning has been that designing a great PBL lesson is something that at best 10% of teachers do well, whereas the majority can deliver a well-designed PBL lesson.

First, it becomes much simpler to hire teachers. You don’t have to have this competing dimension of academic depth and love for children. Just hire the most joyful and present adults to be with students. Don’t worry about degrees, worry about connection and energy.

Fourth, institutional knowledge all gets built into product, making schools much less fragile. The main takeaway from the high-performing charter school networks in my opinion is that when you line up a good approach with exceptional teachers, you can achieve exceptional results. However, when you lose the exceptional teachers, the results revert to the mean.

As a school leader, your job used to be hiring and training teachers. In the future, it will be building the product that fits your school, and then hiring people who love students to bring it to life. The leaders who learn to do both will build schools that get better every year instead of every time they get lucky with a hire.
